k — enter a PID to kill the process
htop — a colorful upgrade to top
kill — send a signal to a process
The sequence: first find the PID with ps aux | grep 进程名, then use kill PID. Use kill -9 only if the process does not respond.
There is no need to look up the PID first, making this more direct than kill.

jobs — list background jobs in the current terminal
+ marks the most recently operated-on job (the default target of fg with no arguments).
fg — bring a background job to the foreground
bg — resume a suspended job in the background
Ctrl+Z — suspend the current foreground task

systemctl manages systemd units and system state. By default, it connects to the system manager; systemctl --user connects to the user manager. User programs can also be managed as user services:
A program you run as a user
systemctl also handles system-level operations such as shutdown, reboot, and suspend:

You can enter poweroff and reboot directly (without the systemctl prefix) because they existed historically as standalone commands. systemd retains them as compatibility entry points. On systemd systems, they are usually handled through those entry points; the specific file or symlink layout depends on the distribution.

This article uses systemctl suspend and systemctl hibernate. Standalone entry points and compatibility commands vary by distribution and installed tools. Hibernation also requires support from the kernel, swap space, and resume configuration.
For more on system services, see Linux login and sessions.
